meta.title: Should Parcelbird launch quick-commerce grocery delivery in 2027?
meta.subtitle: Board discussion document on Parcelbird Now
meta.purpose: Decide whether to launch Parcelbird Now, a 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027

storyline.governing_thought: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should put the cash into its software and reopen quick commerce only if customer sites prove it pays

exec_summary.text: Quick commerce is growing fast, but no operator has yet made it profitable

sub_points.text: US sales grew 2.8 times in three years, to $5.1B in 2025
Both incumbents lose money per order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities

exec_summary.text: At the economics of Parcelbird's own customer sites every order loses money, and pricing does not close the gap

sub_points.text: At the median customer site, each order would lose $6.17
Even best-on-every-driver loses about $1.80 an order; the plan assumes more

exec_summary.text: The plan breaks the 12-month runway floor even on the founders' own numbers

sub_points.text: Spending $9.5M to month 18 leaves about 6 months of runway
At median economics nine stores would lose about $18M a year

exec_summary.text: Scaling the software is the better use of cash; reopen quick commerce only when gates are met

sub_points.text: Software hires use 11% of cash above the floor; the launch needs 132%
Nine late-stage deals would add about $0.9M of ARR, above the $0.8M hires' cost

next_steps.action: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch and stop work on dark-store sites
Make the four software hires and focus sales on the nine late-stage grocers
Build store-based fast-delivery features for grocers in the pipeline
Set a burn plan that keeps 12 months of runway and a path to profitability within current cash
Report the four gates to the board each quarter, starting with customer-site economics

constraints.item: Keep at least 12 months of runway at all times
constraints.effect: the founders' plan leaves about 6 months at month 18; the options table measures every option against the $7.2M above the floor

constraints.item: No new funding round for a delivery operator (lead investor: unlikely)
constraints.effect: the plan must fit inside $12.0M; there is no backstop if losses run above plan

constraints.item: Software business burns $0.4M a month today
constraints.effect: at today's burn the floor is reached in month 18 even with no new spending; if the $9.5M excludes this burn, cash runs out before month 18

constraints.item: Investors want a path to profitability within current cash
constraints.effect: the recommendation adds a burn plan as a next step; the pack has no cost breakdown to size it

constraints.item: Founders' $9.5M rests on plan unit economics above any observed site
constraints.effect: at median economics nine stores would lose about $18M a year

constraints.item: Rider minimum pay standards under consideration in two of the three cities
constraints.effect: would raise rider cost, the largest per-order cost; not sized because the pack gives no level; it is gate 4

alternatives.option: One Columbus dark store for a year before committing to nine
alternatives.why: about $2.6M, 37% of the cash above the floor, to re-test economics that 14 customer sites and the pop-up already show; a store at the median still loses money

alternatives.option: Launch with Zipcart-style pricing ($3.99 fee, promotions at 1%)
alternatives.why: a median site still loses $1.05 an order; break-even needs about 1,042 orders a day, so it becomes the reopening gate instead of a launch case

failure_threshold.driver: orders a day a store holds with a $3.99 fee and 1% promotions at median rider speed
failure_threshold.threshold: above about 1,042 orders a day (16% above the median, 3.7 times the pop-up) a store breaks even after store costs, and the case to reopen quick commerce holds
failure_threshold.range: contribution per order after store costs: low −$12.57 (pop-up), base −$6.17 (median), high −$1.76 (best on every driver); only the plan's better-than-best inputs give +$2.02

consistency.headline: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; it should put the cash into its software and reopen quick commerce only if customer sites prove it pays
consistency.fix: the software case is stated as covering the hires' cost, not as a full path to profitability, which needs a burn plan

gap.target: a path to profitability within current cash while keeping 12 months of runway
gap.base_case: at today's burn the floor is reached in month 18; late-stage deals cover the hires but not the $0.4M monthly burn

closers.option: Convert the software pipeline (37 grocers, $3.55M of ARR) with the four hires
closers.size: gross profit of about half a year's burn plus hires

closers.option: A burn plan approved by the board in Q1 2027
closers.size: not sized: the pack has no cost breakdown

cases.base: software hires cost $0.8M a year, 11% of the cash above the floor; late-stage deals add ARR of 1.1 times that cost
cases.stress: no late-stage deal closes: the hires bring the floor date forward from month 18 to about month 15, still far ahead of the launch, which breaks the floor

gates.metric: orders a day at a customer site with a $3.99 fee and 1% promotions
gates.response: reopen with a one-store test sized inside the headroom
hold hires and cut discretionary spend

gates.metric: new ARR signed from late-stage deals
gates.threshold: $0.8M by end of 2027; under half by mid-2027
gates.response: hold the second pair of hires

gates.threshold: adopted in any of the three cities; each $1 an hour on rider pay adds about $0.42 an order at median speed
gates.response: re-run the break-even before any reopening

lead_message.text: Demand is real: US quick-commerce grocery sales grew 2.8 times in three years, to $5.1B in 2025

sidebar.header: The founders are right that the market is growing fast
sidebar.caption: times the 2022 level, three years later
bullets: **Every year:** growth ran between 38% and 44%, in line with the founders' growth claim
**2025:** the fastest dollar gain of the period, so demand is still accelerating
**Midwest:** the pack has no regional split, so "nobody owns the Midwest" is untested

footnotes: GMV = gross merchandise value of quick-commerce grocery orders in the US; no regional breakdown is available

lead_message.text: Yet no operator has turned that growth into profit, and the regional one is already retreating

body.assumptions_header: Zipcart's result needed top-of-range density, which the pop-up was far from
assumptions: Riders keep the median pace of 2.4 orders an hour, and the fee is kept in full
Volume falls 14% after the fee: 900 orders a day become about 774
Break-even with these fixes needs about 1,042 orders a day, 16% above the median and 3.7 times the pop-up's 280
At the best site's 1,400 orders a day, the same fixes would earn about $0.41, close to Zipcart's $0.40

slides.so_what: Pricing can turn the order positive only where a store already fills to the top of the benchmark range
